scenes.heading: Design a Recommendation Pipeline
scenes.subheading: From viewing events to personalized rows
scenes.narration: Let us design a pipeline that turns billions of viewing and interaction events into the personalized recommendation rows a streaming service shows each member.

scenes.heading: What the pipeline must do
bullets: Capture plays, pauses, and ratings at scale
Build features for users and titles
Train ranking models on fresh data
scenes.narration: The pipeline must capture a firehose of interaction events like plays, pauses, skips, and ratings. It must transform those into meaningful features describing each member's tastes and each title's characteristics. It needs to train and retrain ranking models on fresh data so recommendations keep improving. And it must serve those model predictions with very low latency so the home screen personalizes instantly when a member opens the app.

scenes.heading: The offline-to-online flow
steps: Store features in a feature store
scenes.narration: Interaction events are collected into the data lake as the raw record. Batch jobs compute user and title features over that history and write them into a feature store that both training and serving share. Ranking models are trained and validated on those features and past outcomes. The chosen model is deployed to an online serving layer, which, on each request, reads the latest features from the store and produces a personalized, ranked list of titles for that member.

scenes.heading: Offline training vs online serving
scenes.narration: Offline training runs in batch over enormous history where taking hours is perfectly acceptable, and its goal is maximizing model quality. Online serving must produce a personalized ranking within milliseconds of a request, so its goal is speed and reliability under load. A shared feature store is the crucial link: it guarantees the features used to train the model are the same ones used at serving time, preventing the training-serving skew that silently degrades recommendations.

scenes.heading: The feedback loop
bullets: Log which titles were shown and clicked
Join impressions with outcomes as labels
Retrain so the model keeps improving
scenes.narration: Recommendations improve through a closed feedback loop. The system serves ranked rows to members and logs both what was shown, the impressions, and what members did, the clicks and plays. Those impressions are joined with subsequent outcomes to create training labels that reflect real behavior. The model is periodically retrained on this fresh, labeled data so it adapts to changing tastes. Getting this loop right, and avoiding biases like only learning from what was already shown, is central to quality.

scenes.heading: Evaluating before rollout
bullets: Roll back quickly if metrics dip
scenes.narration: A new model is never trusted blindly. First it is evaluated offline on held-out historical data using ranking metrics to check it beats the current model. Then it is exposed to a slice of live traffic in an A/B test, where real engagement is the ultimate judge. Guardrail metrics on serving latency and catalog coverage ensure the new model is not only more accurate but also fast and diverse. If any metric dips, the platform rolls back quickly to the previous model.

scenes.text: Separate heavy offline training from fast online serving, and unite them with a shared feature store to avoid training-serving skew.
scenes.narration: Cleanly separate heavy offline model training from fast online serving, and unite the two through a shared feature store, because consistent features across both is what keeps recommendations accurate and free of training-serving skew.
